newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina urged to solve Dirty War kidnap of Swede.
newsitem.headline: Argentina urged to solve Dirty War kidnap of Swede.

text.p: Swedish lawmakers on Monday urged Argentina's Congress to clarify the disappearance exactly 20 years ago of a Swedish girl accidentally caught up in the "Dirty War."

A letter from 33 Swedish members of parliament, addressed to Alberto Pierri, head of the lower house of the Argentine Congress, expressed anger at the impunity of the military men suspected of kidnapping and killing Dagmar Hagelin in 1977.

"Those responsible for the disappearance of Dagmar Hagelin, and other people with information about the case, should be called as witnesses," the letter said, referring to "signs that the legal process has come to a standstill."
Pierri's office said there was no official response to the letter because Congress was on vacation until February.

Tireless campaigning by Hagelin's father and pressure from the Swedish government ensured the case became a symbol of the tens of thousands of "disappearances" during the Argentine military's bloody 1976-83 regime.

The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, Argentina's most famous human rights group made up of relatives of "desaparecidos," say the case supports their view that the amnesty for Dirty War criminals decreed by President Carlos Menem shortly after he came to power in 1989 was illegitimate.

Swedish Foreign Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen marked the 20th anniversary of the disappearance by summoning Argentina's envoy in Stockholm to his office on Monday to express Sweden's determination "to clear up the fate of Dagmar Hagelin."

The girl's father Ragmar Hagelin told Argentine television from Sweden that the aim of his 20-year campaign was the same as thousands of Argentine relatives of "desaparecidos" -- to know what happened to his daughter and where her body lies.

"We don't know what happened -- if they killed her, who gave the order, what happened with her remains, and if they can be recovered to be given a decent burial so that we can have a place to cry and place a flower when we feel that human need," he told TodoNoticias cable news, in fluent Spanish.
"This is not just for my daughter, who is my flesh and blood, but also for thousands of others who disappeared who were human beings just as valuable as my daughter," he said.

Ragmar Hagelin believes his daughter was mistaken for a girl wanted by the military at the height of their brutal war against leftist guerrillas and suspected sympathisers. Eyewitnesses have said she was shot by Capt. Alfredo Astiz, known as the "Blond Angel," who has been sentenced to life in jail in France, in absentia, for killing two French nuns the same year Hagelin disappeared.

She is believed to have been taken to the most infamous torture centre, the Navy School of Mechanics, where thousands of detainees were drugged, stripped and thrown into the River Plate on "death flights."
